title: Grouped mean with a missing reading
prompt:
`readings` holds three days of temperature for two sites. One reading
failed and came back missing. Fill the blank so each site gets its mean
temperature.
setup:
library(dplyr)
readings <- data.frame(
  site = c("north", "north", "north", "south", "south", "south"),
  day  = c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3),
  temp = c(18.2, 21.5, NA, 22.1, 23.4, 19.9)
)
hint:
`mean()` takes a second argument that decides what to do when an input
is missing.

solution.code:
readings %>%
  group_by(site) %>%
  summarise(avg_temp = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE))
solution.why:
`mean()` propagates `NA` by default, so a group containing one
missing value returns `NA` for the whole group unless you drop it
explicitly.

checks.on_fail:
The averages don't match. Check that north is averaging its two
real readings rather than all three.
The output columns should be `site` and `avg_temp`.

misconceptions.feedback:
Your code ran without an error, and that's the problem. North came
back `NA` because one of its three readings is missing, and `mean()`
treats one unknown input as making the answer unknown. South is
fine, so half your output looks right — which is exactly how this
slips through review. Add `na.rm = TRUE`.

That gives the right numbers, but it discards north's day 3 row
entirely. If you later summarise a second column from the same
pipeline, that row is gone from it too. `na.rm = TRUE` scopes the
decision to this one calculation.

title: What does the base-R subset return?
prompt:
`readings` still has that missing temperature in north's day 3. How many
rows does this return?

```r
readings[readings$temp > 20, ]
```
setup:
readings <- data.frame(
  site = c("north", "north", "north", "south", "south", "south"),
  day  = c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3),
  temp = c(18.2, 21.5, NA, 22.1, 23.4, 19.9)
)
hint:
Work out what `readings$temp > 20` gives you element by element,
including the missing one. Then ask what `[` does with that value.

options.feedback:
This is the `filter()` answer. `dplyr::filter()` does drop the
missing row — `[` doesn't. The two are not interchangeable, and an
LLM that mixes them inside one script is worth reading closely.

options.text: 4, and one of them is all `NA`
options.feedback:
Right. `NA > 20` is `NA`, not `FALSE`, and `[` responds to an `NA`
index by returning a row of all `NA`s rather than skipping it. You
get a phantom row that came from nowhere in your data.

Four is right but the contents aren't. Only three rows actually
clear 20 — the fourth is the `NA` index, which produces a row of
`NA`s.

options.text: An error, because of the missing value
options.feedback:
Nothing here is invalid, and that's the difficulty. `NA` moves
through comparison and subsetting without complaint, so this fails
quietly instead of loudly.

title: Where does the NA enter?
prompt:
This pipeline returns nothing for north. Click the part of the code
where the missing value first becomes a problem.
hint:
Something here inherits the `NA` rather than creating it. Find the line
that turns a missing *reading* into a missing *result*.

options.feedback:
Yes. North's group contains one `NA`, and `mean()` returns `NA`
whenever any input is `NA`. Everything downstream is working
correctly on a value that is already lost.

`arrange()` does treat `NA` unusually — it sorts missing values
last regardless of direction — but it received the `NA`, it didn't
create it.

The comparison is fine. It's being handed an `NA`, and `NA > 20` is
`NA`, so north drops out of the filter. That's the symptom you
noticed, not the cause.

title: Ask for the summarise call
prompt:
You want an LLM to write the grouped mean from the first exercise, but
you can't paste the data. Write the prompt you'd send.
hint:
The model can't see your data frame. Everything it needs to know about
the shape of your data has to be in the words you send.

response.exemplar:
I have an R data frame called `readings` with columns site (character),
day (numeric) and temp (numeric). Some temp values are NA. Using dplyr,
give me one row per site with the mean temperature, ignoring the
missing values. Call the output column avg_temp.

rubric.criterion: Does the response name the columns it operates on?
rubric.on_fail:
A prompt like "summarise my temperature data" gets you working code
built on invented column names — `temperature`, `location`,
`value`. It looks right, runs against nothing, and reconciling it
takes longer than writing the call yourself.

rubric.criterion: Does the response state that missing values are present in the data?
rubric.on_fail:
Without this, the model has no reason to reach for `na.rm`. You get
code that runs clean and returns `NA` for one group — the exact
failure from the first exercise, now with a second author.

rubric.criterion: Does the response specify dplyr, or otherwise pin the style of R to use?
rubric.on_fail:
Left open, the model picks for you, and it often picks `aggregate()`
or `tapply()`. Not wrong, but it won't match the rest of your
script, and mixed dialects are where subsetting bugs hide.

rubric.criterion: Does the response describe the shape of the desired output, such as one row per site?
rubric.on_fail:
Say what you want back. "Summarise by site" can mean one row per
site or a new column added to all six rows, and those are very
different objects.
